To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Durban Metro Open Space (D-Moss) amendments to town planning schemes were legislative amendments.
the Durban metropolitan open space (D'moss) amendments to town planning schemes are legislative.
The D'Moss amendments were legislative and not executive/administrative.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: what are the limits of municipal legislative and executive powers in relation to the planning function?
the extent to which the Constitution allows local government to legislate in the area of'municipal land use planning'.
the extent of municipal powers over municipal planning, and how the other spheres of governments are affected by these powers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Constitution does not provide for a hierarchy between the three spheres of government in terms of their legislative and executive authority over municipal planning.
the Constitution does not provide for any sphere of government to have legislative authority in respect of'municipal spatial planning'.
the Durban D'Moss amendments are legislative and hence the exclusive domain of provincial government.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
municipal government has the right to exercise executive/administrative powers over spatial planning and land use planning.

the D'Moss amendments to the Durban town planning schemes were legislative amendments, and therefore the Gauteng Development Tribunal had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal against the decision of the Durban Metropolitan Council to approve the amendments.
the national government should refrain from interfering with municipal planning schemes and zoning schemes, except to the extent of ensuring compliance with national environmental laws.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the legislative powers of the provinces and national government are not limited to Part A of Schedule 4 but extend to Part B as well.
there is a need for the South African legislature to clarify the scope of municipal powers over town planning schemes and zoning schemes in particular.
the Constitution is a dynamic document that needs constant interpretation.
